title: Understanding Dataset Distillation via Spectral Filtering
one_liner: Dataset distillation works by matching the frequency-specific patterns of features, and a new method learns both low and high frequencies at once by gradually shifting how patterns are extracted.
lead: When you train a neural network, it learns from many examples. Dataset distillation is a technique that asks: can we compress all those examples down to just a few synthetic ones that teach the model the same lessons? The paper explains why this works by looking at what patterns the network actually needs to learn—distillation boils down to extracting the right frequency information, the same way a radio tuner picks out specific bands. The new method, called Curriculum Frequency Matching, learns both fuzzy patterns and sharp details by gradually shifting its focus as training proceeds.

paras: Training a model usually means showing it thousands or millions of images. Each one takes time to process and memory to store. A natural question: do we really need all of them? Could we distill the dataset down to just a handful of synthetic examples that teach the model the same lessons?

Researchers have built many different distillation methods. Some focus on matching gradients (the direction nudges during training), others on matching feature activations (the internal patterns the model learns). But these methods seem to work in completely different ways. A beginner might assume each method requires its own theory and best practices. What is really happening inside these different approaches?

callout.html: The paper reveals that all dataset distillation methods are secretly doing the same thing: picking out specific frequency bands from the patterns the network sees.

steps.b: Curriculum shifts the focus over time
steps.text: Start with low-frequency patterns, gradually shift toward high-frequency details as training progresses.

paras: Most dataset distillation methods use a fixed strategy throughout training: they extract one specific type of frequency information and stick with it. The paper proposes something new: gradually shift which frequencies you extract as training proceeds. Early on, pull out the blurry, low-frequency patterns. Later, shift toward the sharp, high-frequency details.
object.object: Which frequency bands get extracted from patterns

hidden.name: Frequency information in correlations
paras: When the network processes images, different parts of the learned patterns vary slowly (gradual changes across the image) or quickly (sharp boundaries and textures). These are the frequencies. Mathematically, you can split any pattern into low, medium, and high frequency bands, just like an audio equalizer splits sound into bass, mids, and treble.

The paper measures this by looking at eigenvalues (just special numbers that describe how aligned one dimension is with others). Different distillation methods apply different filters—mathematical operations—to these numbers. A low-pass filter keeps only the slow-changing patterns and drops the sharp ones. A high-pass filter does the opposite.

heat.caption: Darker means more of that frequency is present. Lighter (blurry) appears early, darker (sharp) needs later training.

reads.html: The patterns the network learns can be split into slow-changing (blurry, low-frequency) and fast-changing (sharp, high-frequency) components. Different distillation methods focus on different slices of this spectrum.

The paper interprets each DD objective as a filter applied to the eigenvalues of the feature-feature correlation (a table of how aligned each pattern dimension is with others), extracting specific frequency information from the feature-label correlation.

mechanism.h2: Why matching all frequencies works better
paras: A model needs both types of information to work well. The low-frequency, blurry patterns teach it the broad structure—what is foreground, what is background, what category does this belong to. But the high-frequency, sharp patterns teach it the fine details—which exact textures matter, where the edges are, what distinguishes one dog breed from another.

If you distill with only low-frequency information, your synthetic examples teach the model the big picture but not the details, so it makes crude mistakes. If you distill with only high-frequency information, the model gets the textures right but loses the semantic meaning. By starting with low-frequency patterns and gradually shifting toward high-frequency patterns as training progresses, Curriculum Frequency Matching gives the model the semantic foundation first, then layers in the precision, exactly the way learning actually works best.

math.words: Each distillation objective is a filter applied to the eigenvalues of a correlation matrix. Low-pass filters pick small eigenvalues (slow-changing patterns). High-pass filters pick large eigenvalues (fast-changing patterns). The curriculum method gradually adjusts a learnable parameter to shift between them.
math.equation: L_distill = distance( F(lambda) applied to FFC_matrix, target_FLC_patterns )
symbols: a filter function applied to eigenvalues; different DD methods use different filters
the eigenvalues of the feature-feature correlation matrix
feature-feature correlation: how much each learned pattern dimension aligns with others
feature-label correlation: which patterns predict the correct category
the loss (error) when distilled examples fail to match target patterns

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the correlation table has special alignment numbers [0.1, 0.3, 0.8, 1.5, 2.1].
A low-pass filter might keep only [0.1, 0.3, 0.8] (the slow patterns) and drop [1.5, 2.1].
A high-pass filter would do the opposite: keep [1.5, 2.1] (the fast patterns) and drop [0.1, 0.3, 0.8].
Curriculum Frequency Matching starts like a low-pass filter, then gradually shifts weights: epoch 10 keeps 80% low + 20% high, epoch 50 keeps 30% low + 70% high, epoch 100 keeps 10% low + 90% high.
The distilled images are optimized so that when you process them, they produce those weighted-frequency alignment numbers.

math.note: Different distillation methods are just different filter shapes applied to the same underlying data structure—they all extract specific frequencies, but Curriculum Frequency Matching learns to extract all frequencies by gradually turning a dial.

charts.title: Fixed low-pass distillation
charts.note: Learns the big picture well but misses fine details.

charts.title: Fixed high-pass distillation
charts.note: Learns textures well but loses semantic understanding.

charts.title: Curriculum Frequency Matching
charts.note: Balances both types of information so the model learns well across all kinds of patterns, because starting with low-frequency structure gives semantic grounding while shifting to high-frequency details adds precision.

items.html: If you commit to only low-frequency patterns from the start, the model will never learn fine details, even if you train longer. The synthetic examples simply do not contain that information.
If you shift toward sharp, high-frequency patterns too early, the model has no semantic foundation to build on. It learns texture patterns that do not generalize to different datasets.

Naively creating synthetic examples that are just random pixel values will not capture the learned patterns. You must measure and match the actual correlation structure the real training data creates.

By measuring the frequency content via eigenvalues and gradually shifting the filter, the model learns the semantic structure first, then layers precision on top, matching how human perception actually works—outline first, details later.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement Curriculum Frequency Matching on a small dataset like CIFAR-10. Create a set of synthetic distilled images by optimizing them to match the frequency-weighted correlation patterns of the real training set. Train a simple model (like ResNet-18) on these distilled images only. Compare the accuracy against (1) training on the full real dataset, (2) training on fixed low-pass distilled images, and (3) training on fixed high-pass distilled images.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy of model trained on CFM distilled images minus accuracy of model trained on full real dataset
demo.closing: The demo must show that CFM closes the gap between synthetic and real data better than any fixed-frequency method, because the gradual curriculum strategy gives the model both semantic foundation and fine-grained precision.
